::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How do I solve $ \int_{0}^{1}\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^2}}dx$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4659849/how-do-i-solve-int-01-fracx2-sqrt3x2dx), asked by [Matheman](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/117904/matheman) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-03-15; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I had to solve this integral:
>
> $$\int_{0}^{1}\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^2}}\mathrm{d}x$$
> by the substitution $x=\sqrt{3}t$ the indefinite integral can be written as:
> $$\int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^2}}\;\mathrm{d}x = \int \frac{3t^2}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}\; \mathrm{d}t$$
> at this stage I performed the substitution $\displaystyle t=\frac{e^u-e^{-u}}{2}$, but the computations are definitely too tough for being a high school exercise.
> I'd like to know if there's a simpler method, by substitution, that allows to solve it.
:::

The trigonometric route is to substitute $x = \sqrt{3}\tan\theta$, $dx = \sqrt{3} \sec^2\theta\,d\theta$. Then $\sqrt{3 + x^2} = \sqrt{3} \sec\theta$ and we get
$$\begin{aligned}
    \int_0^1 \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{3+x^2}}\,dx 
    &= \int_0^{\pi/6} \frac{3\tan^2\theta \sqrt{3}\sec^2\theta}{\sqrt{3} \sec\theta}\,d\theta
\\  &= \int_0^{\pi/6} 3\sec\theta\tan^2\theta\,d\theta
\end{aligned}$$
At this point you can either:

* Integrate by parts with $u=\tan\theta$ and $dv = \sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta$. The new integral is a multiple of $\sec^3\theta$.
* Substitute $\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta-1$ so the integrand is a multiple of $\sec^3\theta - \sec\theta$

Both $\int \sec\theta\,d\theta$ and $\int\sec^3\theta\,d\theta$ are “standard” memorizable (or lookupable) functions. We get

$$\begin{aligned}
     3\int_0^{\pi/6} \left(\sec^3\theta-\sec\theta\right)\,d\theta
    &= 3\left[\frac{1}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta - \ln\left|\sec\theta+\tan\theta\right|\right]^{\pi/6}_0
    \\&= \frac{3}{2} \left(\sec\frac{\pi}{6}\tan\frac{\pi}{6} - \ln \left( \sec\frac{\pi}{6}+\tan\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right)
    \\&= \frac{3}{2} \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} - \ln \left( \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right)
    \\&= 1 - \frac{3}{4} \ln 3
\end{aligned}$$
